labels.name: credentials
labels.description: Email/password, magic-link, OTP, phone, username, passkeys

items.body: Closes #11747 ## Summary The phone number plugin's `verifyOTP` callback is called for two distinct operations — phone number verification (`/phone-number/verify`, `consumePhoneNumberOTP`) and password reset (`/phone-number/reset-password`) — but receives no context about which one triggered it. Apps that route to different provider services depending on the purpose (e.g. a separate Twilio Verify service per operation) cannot distinguish the two calls and must fall back to a single shared service or maintain out-of-band state. ## Change `verifyOTP` now receives a third field, `type: "phone-verification" | "password-reset"`, alongside `phoneNumber` and `code`. The type is set at the call site: - `"phone-verification"` — `/phone-number/verify` and `consumePhoneNumberOTP`. - `"password-reset"` — `/phone-number/reset-password`. The shared helper `verifyWithCustomVerifier` accepts `type` as a parameter so that all three call sites stay in sync and cannot drift. The type `PhoneNumberOTPType` is exported from the package for apps that want to type-guard their own code. The docs for `verifyOTP` now document the `type` field and update the example to show routing to different Twilio Verify services based on the purpose. ## Compatibility Adding a field to an object parameter is backwards-compatible: existing `verifyOTP` implementations that destructure only `{ phoneNumber, code }` continue to compile and run without changes. The changeset is marked `minor` because it is a new option field. ## Tests In the `custom verifyOTP` suite of `phone-number.test.ts`: - All existing `toHaveBeenCalledWith` assertions are updated to include the expected `type`, confirming the field is passed correctly in every path. - `should distinguish verification and password reset via type in verifyOTP` (new, `@see #11747`): a single mock verifier records every `type` it receives. The test drives phone verification via `phoneNumber.verify`, server-side consumption via `consumePhoneNumberOTP`, and password reset via `phoneNumber.resetPassword`, then asserts the recorded sequence is `["phone-verification", "phone-verification", "password-reset"]`. This fails on `main` because the `type` field is absent. --- ## Summary by cubic Closes #11747. The phone number plugin's `verifyOTP` callback now receives a `type` field (`"phone-verification"` or `"password-reset"`) alongside `phoneNumber` and `code`, so apps can route phone verification and password-reset codes to different provider services. `/phone-number/reset-password` now checks the code with `verifyOTP` when configured; before it always compared against the code Better Auth generated, so apps using a provider like Twilio Verify couldn't reset passwords. Adding the field is backwards-compatible: existing callbacks that destructure only `{ phoneNumber, code }` keep working. The branch also carries a batch of fixes and features that have since landed on `main`: - Password resets and changes now revoke sessions and save the new password atomically, and the reset token or OTP is consumed only after the new password validates. - Session writes to secondary storage are deferred until the sign-up or reset commits, and session listing falls back to the database when the cache entry is missing. - OAuth provider: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` compatibility, host-bearing custom-scheme native redirects, managed-client disable, resource linking at registration, `clientId` in privilege checks, and startup resilience when resource seeding fails. - SSO: partial mappings accepted, mismatched OIDC issuers rejected, email claims as arrays supported, SAML cert and `callbackUrl` updates allowed with linked accounts, Atlassian named in user-info error logs. - SCIM: attribute names matched case-insensitively, `null` values accepted, inactive users reprovisioned in place, and `409` returned on uniqueness races. - Adapter fixes: Drizzle supports dates in string columns, Mongo aborts failed commits, and Kysely allows concurrent D1 queries. - Works toward lazy AsyncLocalStorage loading on Workers, stops double-decoding magic link callback URLs, and includes `skipLibCheck: false` type fixes, SvelteKit 3 peer support, and docs updates (Effect guide, OAuth resources, community plugins). Written for commit e589913d3ee98c55178b6955649c07f252467207. Summary will update on new commits.

items.title: Allow `customSession` to hide session data from client API without altering server-side `getSession()` for security reason

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Problem

Let's assume both the `user` and `session` objects contain sensitive/internal data and should not be exposed through the client-facing session API.

Based on the documentation, the `customSession` plugin appears to be the appropriate way to control what is returned by `/api/auth/get-session`.

For example:

```ts
customSession(async ({ user, session }) => {
	return {
		user: {},
		session: {}
	};
})
```

This works as expected for the client-facing endpoint: I can confirm that `/api/auth/get-session` no longer exposes the original `user` or `session` fields.

However, there is an unwanted side effect: the result of the server-side API

```ts
auth.api.getSession()
```

is also transformed by `customSession`.

In my use case, I only want to restrict what is exposed to the browser. On the server, I still need access to the complete `user` and `session` objects.

Ideally, the behavior would be:

```text
Browser:
GET /api/auth/get-session
→ sanitized/custom session response

Server:
auth.api.getSession(...)
→ full internal user + session objects
```

Based on the current documentation/API, I don't see a way to achieve this separation.

## Cookie Cache

There is a related issue when `cookieCache` is enabled.

Even when `customSession` removes these fields from the `/api/auth/get-session` response, the cookie cache still contains the `user` and `session` data and sends it to the browser.

This effectively bypasses the intention of `customSession` if the goal is to prevent this information from being exposed client-side.

Using the `jwe` cookie cache strategy mitigates the exposure by encrypting the cached payload, but the underlying problem remains: `customSession` does not appear to control what data is included in the cookie cache.

items.title: fix(generic-oauth): cache discovery and bound discovery requests

labels.name: oauth
labels.description: Social providers, OAuth flows, generic-oauth, oauth-proxy

labels.name: docs
labels.description: Documentation, demos

items.body: ## Summary `genericOAuth` fetches OIDC discovery inside `init`, and `betterAuth()` starts `init` eagerly. Runtimes that construct an auth instance per request (Cloudflare Workers) therefore fetched the discovery document on every request, uncached and with no timeout lever. This change caches successful discovery documents, shares the JWKS resolver, and bounds discovery requests. Closes #10999. ## What changed - **Discovery cache** — successful documents are reused for 5 minutes (the same TTL as the core JWKS cache), keyed by discovery URL + `discoveryHeaders`. The cache is module-level, so every auth instance in the same process or isolate shares it. - Concurrent constructions join one in-flight fetch. - A pending fetch that outlives its own timeout is not joined forever (Workers cancel request I/O when the request ends). - Failures are not cached, so the existing retry-on-first-use behavior from #11750 still recovers immediately. - Client ID is intentionally not part of the key: discovery documents are client-independent, and keying by it would only split the cache into identical entries. - **JWKS resolver cache** — one `createRemoteJWKSet` per `jwks_uri` across auth instances. jose keeps the key set fresh and handles rotation. - **`discoveryTimeout`** — new per-provider option, default `10000` ms (matches the SSO plugin and the previous retry bound). It applies to the initial discovery fetch and retries, and aborts the body as well as the response headers. - **Tests** — 6 new tests in `generic-oauth.test.ts`: shared cache across instances, in-flight sharing, TTL expiry, header-based keying, hanging-discovery abort, and JWKS resolver reuse. Cache state is reset between tests so existing tests that mock the same URL with different responses keep working. - **Docs + changeset** — documented the cache and the new option; `minor` changeset for `better-auth`. ## Behavior notes - A discovery endpoint that takes longer than `discoveryTimeout` is now treated as unavailable instead of blocking initialization indefinitely. - A successful but unusable document (for example, a malformed `jwks_uri`) stays cached for up to 5 minutes, so recovery after the IdP fixes it is bounded by the TTL. - Negative caching/backoff while an IdP is down is intentionally out of scope; #11750 left that for a follow-up because immediate retry-on-use is the current contract. ## Verification - `pnpm typecheck` — passed - Biome — clean - `packages/better-auth/src/plugins/generic-oauth/generic-oauth.test.ts` — 138/138 passed - Other genericOAuth consumers (oauth-popup, anonymous, last-login-method, oauth-provider, private-key-jwt-e2e, account, sign-out) — 179/179 passed - With the pre-fix behavior simulated, 5 of the 6 new tests fail. ## Breaking changes None. `discoveryTimeout` is additive; the default 10s bound matches the retry bound that already existed and the SSO plugin default. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #10999: `genericOAuth` now caches OIDC discovery documents and JWKS resolvers shared across auth instances in the same process or isolate, so runtimes that construct an auth instance per request (Cloudflare Workers) stop fetching provider metadata on every request. Discovery requests are also bounded by a new `discoveryTimeout` option. **Behavior notes** - Successful documents expire after 5 minutes (the same TTL as the core JWKS cache) and are keyed by discovery URL plus `discoveryHeaders`; concurrent constructions share one in-flight fetch. - A discovery endpoint that exceeds `discoveryTimeout` (default 10 seconds, applies to retries) is aborted and treated as unavailable instead of blocking initialization indefinitely. - Failures are not cached, preserving immediate retry-on-use; a successful but unusable document lingers only up to the TTL. - No breaking changes: `discoveryTimeout` is additive with the previous 10-second retry bound as default. Written for commit dc96d5c2d13c8bce32ffab774fc084a8218af1c2. Summary will update on new commits.

items.title: fix(session): do not restore a revoked session from a stale cache

labels.name: database
labels.description: Database layer, all adapters, schema, migrations

labels.name: devtools
labels.description: CLI, OpenAPI, telemetry, i18n, test-utils

items.body: Closes #11585 Session refresh wrote the cached session before it updated the database. With an eventually consistent cache, that write put a revoked session back for the full session lifetime. The next request accepted it. When a session is stored in the database as well as the cache: - Refresh updates the database first, and only while the row is still live. - The row returned by that write is mirrored to the cache before the `update.after` hooks run. Nothing is read back, so a lagging read replica cannot sign out a new session. - If no live row matches, the cached key and its active session list entry are removed. A before hook that rejects the update leaves the cache as is. - Sign-out deletes the cached key again after the row is deleted or ended. A refresh that runs during the session delete hooks cannot restore it. - A profile update loads the user's session rows with one query, then checks each cached key right before it writes. It always writes the database row. When the cached expiry is later, it rereads the row, so a refresh during the sweep keeps its longer expiry and a shortened session stays short. A lagging replica that still returns a revoked row finds the key already deleted by sign-out. Ended rows are removed. Missing rows are skipped and keep their list entry, because a replica may not have a new row yet. - A profile update raises a list entry to the written expiry, so user-wide revocation can still find the cached session. - Writes with a TTL of 0 are skipped, because some stores treat 0 as no expiry. Sessions stored only in the cache keep the base behavior: each cached copy is read and written back in one step. Writes with a TTL of 0 are skipped. This PR also fixes the Drizzle adapter on MySQL. After an update, it rereads the row with the new values swapped into the `where` clause. A range guard such as `expiresAt > now` became `expiresAt > newExpiresAt` and missed the row, so every refresh returned null. It now swaps in values for equality matches only. ## Known Limits `SecondaryStorage` has no compare-and-set, so two windows remain: - A revocation that lands between the refresh's database write and its cache write can still recreate the key. - The active session list is a read-modify-write, like every other writer of that list. ## Testing - Stale cache reproduction: after refresh, the cache does not hold the revoked session, and the following read returns no session. - A refresh mirrors the updated row to the cache and list. - A refresh on a missing row removes the cached key and list entry. - An update hook that rejects the write leaves the cache in place. - An ended preserved session is not extended. - An update hook that revokes the session does not get it restored. - A refresh that runs while the session is being revoked does not restore it. - A profile update keeps a session created during the sweep. - A profile update does not restore a session signed out while it reads the rows. - A profile update keeps a refresh that lands while it reads the rows. - A profile update does not extend a shortened session from a stale cached copy. - A profile update writes the database expiry to the cache and list. - A profile update does not recreate a deleted session. - A profile update skips the write for a session with less than 1 second left. - Drizzle MySQL rereads keep range guards and swap in new values for equality matches. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes session refresh and profile updates restoring a revoked session from a stale secondary storage cache. Session refresh updates the database first and mirrors the returned row to the cache before `update.after` hooks run. A missing or ended row removes the cached key and its active-sessions entry. Profile updates now read the database rows first, then check each cached key right before writing, so a lagging read replica that still returns a revoked row cannot restore it; without a database they read and write each cached copy in one step. When a cached expiry is later than the row, the sweep rereads the row, so a refresh that lands after the row read is kept and a shortened session is not extended. Sign-out deletes cached keys again after the database rows are removed. - List entries are kept as long as their cached keys so user-wide revocation can still find sessions, and writes with a TTL of 0 are skipped. - Drizzle on MySQL, in both the main adapter and the `relations-v2` entry, now swaps updated values into the `where` clause for equality matches only, so a range guard like `expiresAt > now` still matches the updated row. The adapter suite now checks this too. **Known Limits** `SecondaryStorage` has no compare-and-set, so a revocation that lands between a refresh's database write and its cache write can still recreate the key, and the active-session list is a read-modify-write like every other writer of that list. Written for commit da8aed78dc2d9b6ee681fc42fd2339c311839d04. Summary will update on new commits.

items.title: feat(session): allow custom encrypt/decrypt for JWE cookie cache

labels.name: core
labels.description: Core infra, API routes, session, cookies, client SDK

items.body:
## Summary

Adds an opt-in `crypto: { encrypt, decrypt }` option on `BetterAuthOptions`. When set **and** `session.cookieCache.strategy === "jwe"`, the built-in JWE codec is bypassed: the session payload is JSON-stringified, handed to `encrypt`, and the returned ciphertext is what's stored in the cookie. `decrypt` must return the original JSON string.

The use case is delegating session-cookie encryption to a KMS / HashiCorp Vault Transit so the application never holds the encryption key.

**Strict scope.** The hook is only consumed by the JWE cookie cache. Every other use of symmetric crypto in the library (OAuth tokens, 2FA secrets, JWKS rows, OAuth state cookie, OIDC codes, email-otp, oauth-proxy) continues to use `secret` / `secrets` and is untouched.

**No fallback.** When the hook is configured, in-flight cookies issued before the switch fail to decode and fall through to the database / secondary storage on the next read — normal cookie-cache miss behavior. No persisted data is impacted.

## Changes

- `packages/core/src/types/init-options.ts` — new optional `crypto` field on `BetterAuthOptions`.
- `packages/core/src/types/context.ts` — matching optional `crypto` field on `AuthContext`.
- `packages/better-auth/src/context/create-context.ts` — passes `options.crypto` onto the context.
- `packages/better-auth/src/crypto/jwt.ts` — new `hookEncodeSession` / `hookDecodeSession` helpers (JSON envelope with `iat` / `exp` / `jti`, clock-tolerant `exp` enforcement, `null` on failure to match `symmetricDecodeJWT`).
- `packages/better-auth/src/cookies/index.ts` — branches the JWE encode (line ~204) and the standalone `getCookieCache` decode (~510). `secret` stays required for `compact` / `jwt` strategies.
- `packages/better-auth/src/api/routes/session.ts` — branches the JWE decode on session retrieval.
- `packages/better-auth/src/api/routes/session-jwe-hook.test.ts` — new test file with 7 cases.

## Example

\`\`\`ts
betterAuth({
  session: { cookieCache: { enabled: true, strategy: "jwe" } },
  crypto: {
    encrypt: async (plaintext) => /* fetch Vault transit/encrypt */,
    decrypt: async (ciphertext) => /* fetch Vault transit/decrypt */,
  },
});
\`\`\`

## Test plan

- [x] \`pnpm typecheck\` passes (repo-wide).
- [x] New: \`vitest run packages/better-auth/src/api/routes/session-jwe-hook.test.ts\` — 7 / 7 passing.
  - hook roundtrip (encrypt on sign-in, decrypt on \`getSession\`)
  - expired hook payload → \`getSession\` returns null
  - decrypt throws → \`getSession\` returns null (no silent fallback)
  - cookie value is hook ciphertext, not a compact JWE (\`eyJ…\`); plaintext fed to the hook is the JSON envelope
  - \`decrypt\` is called on every cached \`getSession\`
  - tampered ciphertext → \`getSession\` returns null
  - hook is **not** called when strategy is \`compact\`
- [x] Regression: \`vitest run -t "JWE strategy"\` — pre-existing 4 cases in \`session-api.test.ts\` still pass.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- This is an auto-generated description by cubic. -->
---
## Summary by cubic
Adds an opt-in `crypto: { encrypt, decrypt }` hook for the JWE session cookie cache so apps can delegate cookie encryption to a KMS/Vault. Hooks can be sync or async, and docs now clarify ciphertext must be cookie-safe ASCII for chunking.

- New Features
  - Added `crypto` to `BetterAuthOptions` and `AuthContext`; JWE cookie read/write branches to it. `getCookieCache` accepts `crypto` and doesn’t require `secret` with the hook; `secret` is still required for `compact`/`jwt`.
  - Introduced `hookEncodeSession`/`hookDecodeSession` with a JSON envelope (`iat`, `exp`, `jti`) and clock-tolerant `exp` checks; failures return null.
  - Hooks support synchronous or async functions (`Awaitable<string>`), no Promise wrapping needed.
  - Documented ciphertext requirements for `encrypt` output: printable ASCII/base64url, no cookie delimiters/whitespace, and byte-splittable for safe chunking.

- Migration
  - Enable by setting `session.cookieCache.strategy: "jwe"` and providing `crypto.encrypt`/`crypto.decrypt` in `betterAuth(...)`.
  - If calling `getCookieCache` directly, pass the same `crypto` in its config.
  - Switching on an existing deployment invalidates current JWE cookies; requests will fall back to the database on next read. No persisted data is affected.

<sup>Written for commit 3ec7db08003885e85f013216b30a6e116ed57a90. Summary will update on new commits.</sup>

items.title: Date fields are not guaranteed to be Date objects at call sites (systemic adapter date-coercion gap)

labels.name: core
labels.description: Core infra, API routes, session, cookies, client SDK

labels.name: database
labels.description: Database layer, all adapters, schema, migrations

items.body:
## Summary

Throughout the codebase, code that reads a `date`-typed field (`session.createdAt`, `verification.expiresAt`, `key.expiresAt`, and so on) and then constructs a `Date` from it, calls `.getTime()`, or compares it against the current time assumes the adapter returned a real `Date`. That is not guaranteed. Depending on the adapter, the driver, and the storage path, the same field can arrive as a `Date`, an ISO string, a **numeric string** (`"1774295570569"`), or a **number**.

When the value is a numeric string, the `Date` constructor produces `Invalid Date` and downstream arithmetic becomes `NaN`. When it is a plain string, relational comparisons (`field < new Date()`) silently evaluate to `false`. Either way the failure is silent.

This was surfaced by one call site in the `max_age` work (#9936), but it is a data-layer gap, not local to that plugin. There is already a trail of piecemeal fixes for the same root cause (#7937, #3704, #8104, #8105) and open issues touching adjacent facets (#8619, #8882).

## Root cause

The only central coercion is the adapter factory's read transform, and it leaks three ways:

1. It runs only when `supportsDates === false`, but the default is `true` ([factory.ts#L67](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/core/src/db/adapter/factory.ts#L67)), so Prisma, MongoDB, Memory, and Kysely/postgres|mysql trust the driver's return type with no coercion at all.
2. It matches only `typeof value === "string"` and uses a bare `Date` constructor ([factory.ts#L361-L365](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/core/src/db/adapter/factory.ts#L361-L365)), so a `number` is never coerced and a numeric string becomes `Invalid Date`.
3. Secondary storage and the cookie session cache serialize to JSON and never run the adapter transform on read, so dates come back as strings or numbers.

There is no canonical date-normalization in `@better-auth/core`. Instead there are several private reinventions: `normalizeTimestampValue` and `resolveSessionAuthTime` in oauth-provider ([utils/index.ts#L71](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/oauth-provider/src/utils/index.ts#L71), [#L111](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/oauth-provider/src/utils/index.ts#L111)), `deserializeApiKey` in api-key, `toDate` in cimd, and scattered `new Date(...)` wrapping.

This also corrects the premise of #8619, which assumes the runtime "works correctly" by wrapping values in `new Date()`. It does not, for numeric strings.

## Reachability (calibrated)

Default setups are mostly safe: Prisma/Postgres/Mongo return `Date`; the sqlite path coerces ISO strings; `findSession` re-hydrates session expiry; verification entries self-evict via a store TTL. The gap bites with:

- Adapters or drivers that return dates as numeric strings or numbers (better-sqlite3 INTEGER columns, mysql2 with `dateStrings`, custom adapters).
- A few secondary-storage read paths that do not re-hydrate every field (`session.createdAt`/`updatedAt`).

So this is primarily a robustness and adapter-compatibility gap, with a few security-adjacent edges that only activate under those adapters. A maintainer should decide whether any of those edges warrants separate handling; on its own it does not look advisory-grade, because the worst path (verification-token expiry) is mitigated by the store TTL described below.

## Affected call sites

Security-adjacent (wrong security semantics when the date is a string or number):

- OIDC `max_age` and `auth_time`: [oidc-provider/authorize.ts#L308](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/plugins/oidc-provider/authorize.ts#L308), [#L331](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/plugins/oidc-provider/authorize.ts#L331), [oidc-provider/index.ts#L1063](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/plugins/oidc-provider/index.ts#L1063)
- MCP `auth_time`: [mcp/authorize.ts#L208](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/plugins/mcp/authorize.ts#L208), [mcp/index.ts#L759](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/plugins/mcp/index.ts#L759)
- Fresh-session gate for privileged operations (delete account, change email): [session.ts#L643](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/api/routes/session.ts#L643)
- Session expiry comparison: [session.ts#L370](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/api/routes/session.ts#L370) (and the multi-session and OIDC token-expiry paths)

Correctness and crashes:

- JWKS key handling calls `.getTime()` directly and would throw for a string: [jwt/adapter.ts#L25](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/plugins/jwt/adapter.ts#L25), [jwt/index.ts#L192](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/plugins/jwt/index.ts#L192)
- Session field reshaping wraps with a bare `Date`: [internal-adapter.ts#L465](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/db/internal-adapter.ts#L465), [session.ts#L258](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/api/routes/session.ts#L258)

For contrast, the correct pattern already exists in one place: `consumeVerificationValue` hydrates via `hydrateCachedVerification` ([internal-adapter.ts#L1265](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/db/internal-adapter.ts#L1265)), while its sibling `findVerificationValue` returns the raw JSON ([internal-adapter.ts#L1147](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/af572166a26c4c84574ce70f6e850a21a6608d70/packages/better-auth/src/db/internal-adapter.ts#L1147)). The expiry checks on the `findVerificationValue` path (2FA OTP, password reset) would fail open for a string expiry, but the secondary-storage entry self-evicts at its store TTL, so this is not exploitable by default; it only bites a primary DB adapter that returns numeric-string dates.

The oauth-provider plugin already defends its own `max_age`/`auth_time` via `normalizeTimestampValue`. The older oidc-provider and MCP sites above do not.

## Proposed fix

Make the data-layer boundary the single source of truth so call sites can trust a `Date`:

1. Promote `normalizeTimestampValue` into `@better-auth/core` on a stable path (e.g. `@better-auth/core/utils/date`). It already handles `Date`, number, numeric string, and ISO string, and returns `undefined` for genuinely unparseable input.
2. In the factory read transform, coerce **every** `date`-typed field through it, regardless of `supportsDates` (replace the gated bare `new Date(...)`).
3. Re-hydrate dates on the secondary-storage and cookie read paths through the same helper, and update the drizzle `customTransformOutput` similarly.
4. Retire the private reinventions and the scattered `new Date()` wrapping.

This changes the adapter contract to always return a `Date` for `date` fields, which is breaking for any third-party adapter that relied on string pass-through, so it targets `next` with a migration note. It also makes the typing question in #8619 answerable: date fields are `Date`, period.

## Related

- #8619 (types don't reflect `supportsDates`; assumes the runtime is already correct)
- #8882 (drizzle + sqlite INSERT flags, the write path)
- #8618, #3704, #7937, #8104, #8105 (earlier piecemeal coercion fixes)

labels.name: identity

items.body: Closes #11317 ## Summary A refresh-token family is revoked in one update before the deletes, so a successor stays unusable when the refresh-row delete fails. Rotation also drops a new successor if the parent was invalidated again or removed. ## Test plan - [x] `vitest` `refresh family invalidation` in `packages/oauth-provider` - [ ] Replay of a rotated refresh token returns `invalid_grant` for the successor when family invalidation runs - [ ] A normal rotation, where `revoked` and `rotatedAt` stay equal, still issues the successor --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes refresh-token family invalidation in the OAuth provider so a rotated successor can't survive a failed family delete. - Revokes all refresh rows for a (client, user) pair in one update before deleting them, so a failed delete still leaves the family unusable. The revoke also clears the replay cache so the old token can't return a cached successor. - Rotation now re-reads the parent and discards the new successor if the parent was revoked again after rotation or removed. Written for commit a22547454d5d171164d191c11f13019288408180. Summary will update on new commits.

labels.name: organization

items.body: ## Description Synchronize session cookies and client cookie caches across organization lifecycle state transitions (`acceptInvitation`, `createOrganization`, `deleteOrganization`, `removeMember`, and `leaveOrganization`). Previously, active organization and team mutations updated the database session via `adapter.setActiveOrganization(...)` without calling `setSessionCookie(ctx, { session: updatedSession, user: session.user })`. This caused client-side session cookies and cookie caches to remain out of sync with the database, leading to stale organization context and membership resolution failures under concurrent multi-session usage. Fixes #10835 ## Changes - **`acceptInvitation`**: Re-ordered active team handling to avoid premature cookie generation, ensured both active organization and team IDs are updated in session, and invoked `setSessionCookie`. - **`createOrganization`**: Synchronize session cookie when `!keepCurrentActiveOrganization`. - **`deleteOrganization`**: Reset active organization session and synchronize session cookie after organization deletion succeeds. - **`removeMember` & `leaveOrganization`**: Synchronize session cookie to `activeOrganizationId: null` on member self-removal and leaving. - **Non-member fallback**: Synchronize session cookie when resetting active organization prior to throwing `APIError`. - **Tests**: Added comprehensive regression tests in `organization.test.ts` verifying resolved session cookies across all lifecycle operations. - **Changeset**: Added patch changeset for `@better-auth/organization`. ## Type of Change - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) ## Checklist - [x] My code follows the code style of this project - [x] I have added tests that prove my fix is effective - [x] New and existing unit tests pass locally with my changes - [x] I have added a changeset file --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes stale session cookies on organization lifecycle transitions so the client-side session stays in sync with the database session (fixes #10835). Organization operations previously updated the active organization or team in the database session via `adapter.setActiveOrganization(...)` / `adapter.setActiveTeam(...)` without calling `setSessionCookie(...)`, so the session cookie kept the old organization context. `acceptInvitation`, `createOrganization`, `deleteOrganization`, `removeMember`, `leaveOrganization`, and the non-member fallback paths now reissue the session cookie whenever the active organization or team changes. **Behavior notes** - Self-removal, leaving, or deleting the active organization resets the cookie to `activeOrganizationId: null`. - The cookie is left untouched when the active organization doesn't change: deleting a non-active organization, removing another member, or creating an organization with `keepCurrentActiveOrganization: true`. - Adds regression tests covering all lifecycle transitions, including team sync and the session cookie cache, and a patch changeset for `better-auth`. Written for commit 320304dc300bdccfc48837f6c8fb63133fa6b892. Summary will update on new commits.

items.title: fix(cimd): check client_id URL policy before spending fetch budget

labels.name: docs
labels.description: Documentation, demos

items.body:
Closes #11949

## Root cause

`createCimdResolver` takes a metadata fetch permit by calling `acquireMetadataFetchPermit(clientId)` **before** `fetchClientMetadataDocument` runs the pre-fetch gate (`validateClientIdUrl` + `isMetadataDocumentUrlAllowed`). The permit consumes the global and per-origin rolling 60s budgets and creates per-client pacing state. Releasing it only frees concurrency, not the window.

As a result, every refused `client_id` URL spends budget even though nothing is ever fetched. A flood of disallowed or invalid IDs then makes the governor return 429 `temporarily_unavailable` to allow-listed clients.

## Fix

- Extract the gate into `assertClientIdUrlFetchable()` in `client-store.ts`.
- In the resolver, run it for **every caller** that would fetch or join an in-flight fetch, before any fetch permit is taken. Only the permit and the fetch are coalesced. Two consequences:
  - Refused URLs never spend the global or per-origin budget.
  - A context-dependent policy (the hook receives `GenericEndpointContext`) is never skipped because another caller's fetch is already in flight.
- After the gate, the resolver re-reads the cache and then checks `inFlightResolutionByClientId`, with no `await` between that check and registering a new in-flight fetch. A caller whose policy decision resolves late therefore reuses a document cached in the meantime, or joins the in-flight fetch. It never starts a duplicate fetch.
- `fetchClientMetadataDocument` keeps the pure `validateClientIdUrl` check as defense in depth. The application hook runs once per caller.
- If the cache became fresh while this caller's policy was pending (another caller refreshed it), the resolver re-reads the stored client instead of returning the snapshot read before the policy, so fields a refresh removed (for example redirect URIs) are not accepted.
- Fresh-cache hits are unchanged and skip the gate, as on `main`.
- Docs: `cimd.mdx` (governor section and the `isMetadataDocumentUrlAllowed` option) and the hook's JSDoc now say when the hook runs, that it runs before any fetch budget is spent, and that it should be cheap or cache its decisions if it consults an external service.
- Patch changeset for `@better-auth/cimd`.

## Behavior changes worth noting

- **Pacing.** Refused IDs, and a throwing or slow `isMetadataDocumentUrlAllowed` hook, no longer create per-client failure pacing entries (`minimumFetchInterval`), since they are rejected before any fetch. Real fetch attempts still count, including network failures, non-200 responses and 304 revalidations.
- **Hook calls.** The hook now runs once per caller that needs a fetch, including same-client callers that end up sharing one fetch. On `main`, coalesced callers skipped it, and hook calls were bounded only because the fetch budget ran out first, which is the coupling #11949 describes. The `/oauth2/authorize` endpoint rate limiter still applies. If you'd like a separate bound on hook concurrency, I'm happy to add it in a follow-up.

## Tests

Six regression tests in `packages/cimd/src/fetch-governor.test.ts` (each with an `@see` link to this issue), using the existing governor harness. The concurrency tests are deterministic: every policy call returns its own deferred promise, the metadata response is held by a deferred promise, and the tests wait on observable milestones. There are no sleeps.

- **Allow-list flood.** Setup: `maximumFetchesPerMinute: 2`, `maximumFetchesPerOriginPerMinute: 1`, and an allow list that admits only one URL.
  - Requests: 4 IDs on other origins, plus 1 refused URL on the allowed origin, then the allowed client.
  - On `main`: refused `[400, 400, 429, 429, 429]`, and the allowed client gets **429**.
  - With this PR: `[400 ×5]`, then 302 to consent, with exactly one metadata fetch.
- **Invalid-URL flood.** Requests: private/loopback hosts, rejected by `validateClientIdUrl`, then a valid client.
  - On `main`: `[400, 400, 429]`, and the valid client gets **429**.
  - With this PR: `[400 ×3]`, then consent.
- **Coalesced fetch, per-caller policy.** Two same-client callers, `maximumFetchesPerOriginPerMinute: 1`: two policy calls, one fetch, both reach consent.
- **A denied concurrent caller is refused.** While an allowed caller's fetch is in flight, a second caller whose policy returns `false` gets 400. The allowed caller reaches consent, with one fetch.
- **A late policy decision reuses the fresh cache.** The second caller's policy resolves after the first caller fetched and cached the document. It reaches consent without a second fetch.
- **A late policy decision sees the refreshed client.** After the cached document expires, one caller refreshes metadata that drops the redirect URI while a second caller's policy is pending. Neither caller reaches consent with the removed redirect, and there are two fetches in total.

The three concurrency tests fail on `main` and on this PR's first commit. On `main`, coalesced callers never invoke the policy. On the first commit, the late caller got 429. The refreshed-client test fails on 471a937, where the slower caller reached consent with the removed redirect.

Run locally (Node 24.22.0, pnpm 11.1.1):

- `packages/cimd` vitest: 9 files, **207/207 pass** (201 before + 6 new).
- The 6 regression tests, run 20×: **20/20 pass**.
- `e2e/smoke` `node --test test/cimd.spec.ts` against rebuilt cimd: **2/2 pass**.
- `packages/mcp` vitest: 5 files, **92/92 pass**.
- `pnpm typecheck` (repo-wide `tsc --build --force`): pass.
- `pnpm lint` (biome, 1878 files): clean. cspell and remark are clean on the changed files.

This change was made with AI assistance; the tests listed above were run locally before opening this PR.

items.title: oauth-provider: stop writing configured resources at startup and make allowedScopes storable with Prisma

labels.name: target: minor
labels.description: Targets next minor release

labels.name: database
labels.description: Database layer, all adapters, schema, migrations

labels.name: identity
labels.description: OAuth/OIDC provider, device flow

items.body:
## Summary

Two defects in how `@better-auth/oauth-provider` stores protected resources remain after the patch on `main` (#11726). That patch stops startup failures from breaking the auth instance. It does not change what startup does or how `allowedScopes` is stored. Both fixes below change observable behavior, so they target `next` as a minor release.

1. **Startup still reads and writes the database.** The plugin's `init` hook (`oauth.ts`) calls `seedResourcesOnce`, which copies the `resources` config into the `oauthResource` table. `betterAuth()` starts `init` when it is called, which is usually at module import. So importing the auth config touches the database during `next build`, during `auth generate`, and in unit tests that never use OAuth, and a build that has production credentials writes rows to the production database. Startup also waits for the database's connection timeout when the database is slow. The patch keeps this working only through workarounds: it matches error messages to recognize a missing table, and it re-reads the row after a failed insert to detect a concurrent instance.
2. **"No scope restriction" cannot be stored with Prisma.** A resource without `allowedScopes` is written with `allowedScopes: null`, meaning no restriction. With Prisma on PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, or MongoDB, the generated column is a `String[]` list. The following was verified against Prisma 7.8 and PostgreSQL 17:
   - `create` with `allowedScopes: null` is rejected with ``Argument `allowedScopes` must not be null.``
   - Omitting the field stores SQL `NULL`, but Prisma reads it back as `[]`.
   - `resolveResourcePolicy` treats `[]` as an allowlist that matches nothing, so every token request for the resource fails with `invalid_scope`.

   The resource that `mcp()` adds has no `allowedScopes`, so `mcp()` with Prisma needs the documented workaround: declare the resource in `resources` with explicit `allowedScopes`.

Related: #10867 (fully resolved by part 1), #10887 (part 2 removes the startup database access it reports), tracking issue #11538.

## Constraints

- **Client links require a resource row.** `oauthClientResource.resourceId` has a foreign key to `oauthResource.identifier` (`schema.ts`, the `oauthClientResource` model). A configured resource can stay in memory for policy lookups, but linking a client to it needs a row first.
- **`resourceSeedMode` must keep its meaning.** It is public configuration:
  - `insertOnly` (the default): a database row, once it exists, wins over config, so admin edits survive restarts.
  - `merge`: config fields that are present override the row.
  - `overwrite`: config replaces the row.
- **Some code reads `oauthResource` directly** instead of going through `getResource`:
  - `listResourcesEndpoint`, `getResourceByIdentifierEndpoint`, `updateResourceEndpoint`, `deleteResourceEndpoint` and `linkClientResourceEndpoint` in `oauthResource/endpoints.ts`
  - `getResourceCustomClaims` in `resources.ts`

## Proposed approach

The parts are independent and can land as separate PRs.

### Part 1: a storable `allowedScopes` contract

- **Contract:** omitted or `null` means no restriction, and a non-empty array is an allowlist. An empty array is rejected as input, with an error that points to `disabled: true` to stop issuance or `null` to remove the restriction.
- **Validate input** in both places it enters:
  - each object entry in the `resources` config, when the plugin is constructed
  - the admin create and update body (`resourceBodySchema` in `oauthResource/index.ts`)
- **Write** `[]` (or omit the field) for "no restriction" on every adapter. Stop writing explicit `null` in `buildSeedRow` (`resources.ts`) and `buildResourceRow` (`oauthResource/endpoints.ts`). An admin update that clears the restriction writes `[]`.
- **Read** `null`, `undefined` and `[]` as "no restriction" through one helper, used by `resolveResourcePolicy` and any other reader of `allowedScopes`. Once `[]` can no longer be written on purpose, a stored `[]` can only mean "unset".
- **Migration:** rows that hold `[]` today refuse every token. After this change they allow every requested scope. The changeset must say this, and tell users who rely on `[]` to block a resource to set `disabled: true` before upgrading. A config that contains `allowedScopes: []` now fails validation.

### Part 2: no database access during `init`

- **Resolve configured resources in memory.** Build a map of the configured entries, keyed by identifier, when the plugin is constructed. `getResource(identifier)` combines the database row, when one exists, with the configured entry according to `resourceSeedMode`:
  - `insertOnly`: the row if it exists, otherwise the configured entry
  - `merge`: the row, with the configured entry's present fields on top
  - `overwrite`: the configured entry
- **Create rows only when a link needs one.** Add an idempotent `ensureResourceRow(identifier)` that inserts from the configured entry and, if the insert fails, re-reads before rethrowing. Call it before writing `oauthClientResource` links (`persistOAuthClientRegistration` in `register.ts`, and `linkClientResourceEndpoint`). Also call it when an admin updates a configured resource that has no row yet.
- **Make admin and claim readers see configured resources:**
  - `listResourcesEndpoint` returns rows merged with the configured entries that have no row.
  - `getResourceByIdentifierEndpoint` and `getResourceCustomClaims` resolve through the same combine step.
  - `cachedResources` keeps working.
- **Remove** the `init` seeding call, `seedResources`, `seedResourcesOnce` and its seed state, `resetSeedStateForTests`, `logStartupSeedFailure`, and `MISSING_TABLE_PATTERN`. Update the tests that call them: `resources.test.ts`, `resource-discovery.test.ts`, `resources-e2e.test.ts`, `register.test.ts`, `validation-flow.test.ts`, `claim-authority.integration.test.ts`, `oauthResource/endpoints.test.ts`, and `resource-startup.test.ts`.
- **Reword** the `resources` and `resourceSeedMode` JSDoc in `types/index.ts` from "boot-time seeding" to how config combines with database rows.
- **Observable changes for the changeset:**
  - The table no longer contains a row for a configured resource until a client is linked to it or an admin edits it, so tooling that reads the table directly sees fewer rows.
  - `merge` and `overwrite` are applied when a resource is read, not written into stored rows.

## Code markers

The patch on `main` marks every place this work changes with `TODO(#11725)` or `FIXME(#11725)`:
- `oauth.ts`: the `init` seed call
- `resources.ts`: `buildSeedRow`, `resolveResourcePolicy`, `getResource`, `MISSING_TABLE_PATTERN`
- `oauthResource/endpoints.ts`: `buildResourceRow`, `listResourcesEndpoint`
- `oauthResource/index.ts`: `resourceBodySchema`

Remove each marker as its part lands.

## Acceptance

- Constructing `betterAuth()` with `resources` or `mcp({ resource })` makes no adapter call on any OAuth model. Check this with an adapter spy that fails the test on any call.
- `auth generate` succeeds for a Drizzle project whose schema has only the core tables.
- A token request for a configured resource that has no row applies its policy: TTL, `allowedScopes`, `disabled`, and custom claims.
- Two concurrent registrations that link the same configured resource create exactly one `oauthResource` row.
- Prisma on PostgreSQL (e2e adapter suite): a configured resource without `allowedScopes` allows the requested scopes, and `allowedScopes: []` is rejected on input.
- The admin list includes configured resources that have no row.
- `insertOnly`, `merge` and `overwrite` each produce the combined result described above.
- Docs: in `docs/content/docs/plugins/oauth-provider.mdx` (the Resources section), replace the startup-write paragraph and the Prisma callout added by the patch with the new behavior. Remove the Prisma note in `docs/content/docs/plugins/mcp.mdx`.
- A `minor` changeset that lists the migration steps above.

labels.name: core

items.body: ## Summary Adds `organization.transferOwnership`, a dedicated endpoint for handing an organization to another member, with an optional email confirmation (`ownershipTransfer`) that can be switched to `confirmationMode: "explicit"`. Closes #11529 ## Problem Today the only way to change an organization's owner is `update-member-role` with the creator role. It takes effect immediately and is a generic multi-role endpoint, so several things are easy to get wrong: - the default `admin` role includes `member:update`, so an admin can end up creating a second owner while the real owner is untouched - the swap is two role changes, so two racing transfers can leave two owners, and a failure halfway can leave none ## Changes - `POST /organization/transfer-ownership` (`organizationId`, `newOwnerMemberId`, `callbackURL?`). Only a member who actually holds `creatorRole` can call it, not just anyone with `member:update`. - The swap lives in the org adapter (`transferOwnership`). It promotes the target first, keeping any other roles it holds, then demotes the previous owner. Both writes are compare-and-swap updates. The previous owner has to still hold `creatorRole` when the swap starts and again on every demotion attempt, because demoting a row that no longer holds it is a no-op that still reports success: without that, a second transfer that started from a stale view of the owner promotes its target and leaves two owners. A demotion whose guard loses because the owner's role string changed for an unrelated reason is retried with the freshly read role (up to three attempts) instead of being reported as an already completed transfer. - If the demotion can't be applied, or any step after the promotion throws (including the re-read), the promotion is rolled back, guarded on it still holding exactly the role it was given so an unrelated edit to the target isn't overwritten. This is best effort, not atomic: promote and demote are separate rows and the adapter layer has no cross-row transaction that works everywhere, so a third write to the target in between can defeat the rollback, in which case a distinct error asks for a manual review of the owners. - `organizationHooks.beforeTransferOwnership` / `afterTransferOwnership`. - Optional confirmation: with `ownershipTransfer.sendTransferOwnershipVerification` configured, the current owner (not the target) gets a link instead of the swap happening right away. `transferTokenExpiresIn` sets the lifetime. - `"instant"` (default): `GET /organization/transfer-ownership/callback` re-checks everything and applies it. - `"explicit"`: the link is the app's own URL, and the app calls `GET .../preview` then `POST .../confirm`, so a link prefetcher or scanner can't apply it. - The token is validated first and only consumed right before the swap, after the session, the owner's role and the target's eligibility are re-checked. An unauthenticated or unauthorized visit doesn't burn it. It is bound to `(organization, current owner, target member)`, and records the mode it was issued for: `GET .../callback` refuses an `"explicit"` token (before consuming it), so a `callbackURL` naming another trusted host that serves the same auth routes can't turn it into a one-click transfer, and the token stays usable for `confirm`. - The immediate path and the preview, confirm and callback endpoints read the session through `getAuthoritativeSessionFromCtx`, so a revoked session that an earlier hook loaded from the cookie cache can't authorize a transfer. I reproduced this with tests (a hook that preloads the cached session, a revoked session row and a valid cached cookie) before fixing it; a transfer went through. - Preview returns the members' users through `parseUserOutput`, so fields marked `returned: false` aren't exposed. - In explicit mode `callbackURL` must be an absolute URL that doesn't lead back to the instant callback (however its path is encoded) and doesn't already carry a `token` parameter. It's checked before the token is created, so a rejected request leaves no orphaned row. This uses the same small helper, `utils/confirmation-url.ts`, as the delete-user and change-email PRs; the file is identical in all of them so they merge cleanly in any order. - New error codes for the transfer-specific failures, and the client refreshes the active member signals after a transfer. ## Notes for review - `update-member-role` is left alone. - No schema changes and no breaking changes. Without `ownershipTransfer`, the transfer is immediate. - For HTTP requests the origin of `callbackURL` is checked against `trustedOrigins` by the existing origin middleware; direct `auth.api` calls skip that, which the docs call out. ## Tests In `transfer-ownership.test.ts`: - immediate swap, instant confirmation and explicit confirmation (preview doesn't swap, confirm does) - target outside the organization, yourself, already an owner, and a non-owner caller, including an admin who holds `member:update` - the token isn't consumed by a visit with no session, and a rejected attempt by another signed-in member doesn't burn it - expired and replayed tokens, and a token used concurrently, apply once - two concurrent transfers to different targets apply at most one - the target's other roles are preserved, and the permission being revoked after the email was sent is honored - a transfer that starts from an owner a concurrent transfer already demoted is refused and leaves one owner (deterministic, via a hook that completes a second transfer first) - a failing re-read of the owner after a lost demotion guard rolls the promotion back - an explicit-mode token can't be redeemed through the GET callback, and still works afterwards for `confirm` - a revoked session with a valid cached cookie is rejected by preview, confirm and callback (with a hook that preloads the session) - missing, relative, callback-pointing (plain, trailing slash, percent-encoded, dot segments) and `token`-carrying `callbackURL`s are rejected and leave no token - preview doesn't expose `returned: false` user fields - `beforeTransferOwnership` / `afterTransferOwnership` hooks Plus unit tests for the URL helper and the client signals. ## Changeset `better-auth`: `patch` --- ## Summary by cubic Adds `organization.transferOwnership`, a dedicated endpoint for handing an organization to another member, replacing the error-prone route through `update-member-role`. - Only the current holder of `creatorRole` can trigger a transfer, so a regular admin with `member:update` can no longer mint a second owner. - The swap promotes the new owner first (preserving their other roles), then demotes the previous one, with compare-and-swap writes and rollback so concurrent transfers can't leave an organization with two owners or none. The owner must still hold `creatorRole` when the swap starts and on every demotion attempt; a lost race is retried with the freshly read role, and an error during that re-read also rolls the promotion back. - Optional email confirmation sends a link to the current owner; `confirmationMode: "explicit"` makes the link lead to your own page so link scanners can't apply the transfer. - The token is validated first and only consumed right before the swap, so an unauthenticated or unauthorized visit doesn't burn it, and a revoked session from the cookie cache can't authorize it. - The immediate path, callback, preview and confirm all re-read the session store, and explicit-mode tokens record their mode so the GET callback refuses them. The explicit `callbackURL` check canonicalizes the base path too. **Migration** - No schema changes or breaking changes; without `ownershipTransfer` configured, the transfer happens immediately. Written for commit 662c7322e37ccd81b581595a76ad96416522e80c. Summary will update on new commits.

items.body:
## Summary

This PR adds first-class caching for dynamic organization role permissions and introduces a lower-level permission API for callers that already know a member's org roles.

## Closes: #9213 

## What changed

- Added `organization({ permissionCache: { enabled, ttl } })`
- Reused global `secondaryStorage` as the cache layer for dynamic organization role definitions
- Added `auth.api.hasPermissionForRoles(...)` to evaluate permissions from caller-provided roles without a membership lookup
- Refactored organization permission resolution so `hasPermission` and `hasPermissionForRoles` share the same role-loading and caching path
- Added route-level cache invalidation for:
  - org role create
  - org role update
  - org role delete
  - organization delete
- Updated org deletion to explicitly remove `organizationRole` rows before deleting the org
- Documented the new cache option and `hasPermissionForRoles` API
- Added a changeset for a `minor` release

<!-- This is an auto-generated description by cubic. -->
---
## Summary by cubic
Adds caching for dynamic organization role permissions via global `secondaryStorage` with a default 60s TTL and an optional in-memory TTL cache. Introduces `auth.api.hasPermissionForRoles` to check permissions when roles are already known, and enforces auth on all role permission checks. Closes #9213.

- **New Features**
  - `organization({ permissionCache: { enabled, ttl } })` caches dynamic role definitions in `secondaryStorage` (default 60s) and optionally in-memory; validates cache payloads and self-heals if corrupt.
  - In-memory role cache uses TTL and only populates when `useMemoryCache: true`.
  - Warns once and falls back to DB if `permissionCache.enabled` is set without global `secondaryStorage`.
  - `auth.api.hasPermissionForRoles(...)` server endpoint; accepts roles as array or comma string; skips membership lookup.
  - Automatic cache invalidation on org role create/update/delete and organization delete; best-effort and non-blocking if secondary storage invalidation fails.

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Role permission checks now require an authenticated session (including `hasPermissionForRoles`).
  - Organization deletion now removes `organizationRole` rows before deleting the org to prevent leftovers.

items.body:
### Closes #5876

This PR implements improved error handling for the magic link verification endpoint, specifically for mobile clients. Previously, when an invalid token was provided and no errorCallbackURL was set, the backend would default to redirecting to the root path with an error query parameter, which is not suitable for mobile apps. This change ensures that the verify function resolves with a JSON error object (e.g., { code: 'INVALID_TOKEN' }) when called from a mobile client or when no callback URL is provided, allowing proper client-side error handling.

### Changes

- Modified the magic link verification endpoint to return a JSON error object (e.g., { code: 'INVALID_TOKEN' }) when called from a mobile client or when no callback URL is provided.
- Updated OpenAPI metadata to document both JSON and redirect response types.
- Added a check to differentiate between requests from the browser and mobile apps using the x-better-auth-client: mobile header.
- Ensured backward compatibility for web clients by maintaining redirect behavior when a callback URL is provided.
- Added test cases specifically for requests from mobile apps.

### Note: On the mobile client side, users need to send the header x-better-auth-client: mobile in the request.

### Impact

- Mobile clients can now handle errors directly without relying on redirects.
- Web clients continue to receive redirects as before, ensuring no breaking changes for existing integrations.

### Testing Strategy

- Verified that mobile clients receive a JSON error object when an invalid or expired token is provided and no callback URL is set.
- Confirmed that web clients still receive redirects when a callback URL is provided.
- Tested token expiration and other error scenarios to ensure consistent behavior.



<!-- This is an auto-generated description by cubic. -->

items.title: Allow a custom fetch implementation for the SSO plugin's server-side federation requests

labels.name: security
labels.description: 2FA, rate limiting, captcha, HIBP

labels.name: enterprise
labels.description: SSO (OIDC + SAML), SCIM provisioning

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
### What

`@better-auth/sso` issues four server-side requests against operator- and tenant-influenced URLs, and a deployment has no way to route any of them through its own fetch implementation. Please consider an optional `customFetchImpl` (or equivalent fetch-injection seam) on `SSOOptions`, threaded to those call sites and through `validateAuthorizationCode`.

### The four call sites

Verified against `@better-auth/sso` 1.6.25 and `@better-auth/core` 1.6.25 as installed:

1. **OIDC discovery** — `@better-auth/sso/dist/index.mjs:474`, `betterFetch(url, { ... })` against `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration`.
2. **Userinfo** — `@better-auth/sso/dist/index.mjs:3063`, `betterFetch(config.userInfoEndpoint, { ... })`.
3. **Token exchange** — `validateAuthorizationCode` in `@better-auth/core`, which reaches `betterFetch` via `fetchRefusingRedirects` in `dist/oauth2/reject-redirects.mjs`.
4. **JWKS** — `@better-auth/core/dist/oauth2/validate-authorization-code.mjs:73`, `createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(jwksEndpoint), { [customFetch]: ... })`.

`@better-fetch/fetch` already honours `opts.customFetchImpl` (1.3.1, `dist/index.js:220`), so three of the four are a threading problem rather than a design one. The plugin passes literal option objects at every call site and `SSOOptions` exposes no fetch field, so there is nowhere for a caller to supply one.

The JWKS path is the harder case: jose's `[customFetch]` hook is already occupied, and the function bound to it calls the raw global `fetch` rather than `betterFetch`, so it would not pick up a `customFetchImpl` even if one were threaded through the plugin. It probably needs its own pass-through.

### Why it matters to us

We run these against tenant-supplied issuer URLs, so the outbound surface is attacker-influenced by design. We currently bound it with a process-global undici dispatcher — address-class pinning plus `maxResponseSize`, with `allowH2: false` because `maxResponseSize` is enforced only in undici's `client-h1` and appears nowhere in `client-h2`.

That handles socket-level and response-size controls. What it cannot supply is a **total wall-clock deadline**, because that needs an `AbortSignal` at the fetch layer. undici's `bodyTimeout` is an inter-chunk idle timeout, so a host dripping one byte per interval is never timed out; at a 256 KiB cap the worst case is measured in weeks. A fetch seam is the clean fix; a global dispatcher structurally cannot be one.

To be clear about what is **not** being asked: the redirect posture is already good. The plugin sets `redirect: "error"` at both of its own call sites, and core refuses redirects portably via `NO_FOLLOW_REDIRECT` + `assertResponseNotRedirect`. That is stricter than per-hop revalidation and we are not asking for it to change.

### Would you accept a PR?

Happy to open one adding an optional `customFetchImpl` on `SSOOptions`, threaded to the discovery and userinfo call sites and through `validateAuthorizationCode`, with the JWKS hook taking its own pass-through so the existing redirect assertion is preserved. Wanted to check the shape you would prefer before writing it — in particular whether the seam belongs on `SSOOptions` or lower down on the core OAuth2 helpers, since the token and JWKS paths are shared with the social providers.

Closes #5728
# ✨ Feature: Add Last-Used Organization Tracking and Auto-Set on Sign-In 

This PR addresses a common pain point for users belonging to multiple organizations by introducing **native tracking and automatic restoration** of the last-used organization upon sign-in.


---

## 🧩 Problem
When a user belongs to several organizations, the system currently **does not remember** which one they were last active in. This forces users to **manually switch organizations** every time they sign in, which is confusing and inefficient.

## 💡 Solution
We're implementing a robust mechanism to track and automatically restore the user's last active organization:
* A new `lastUsed` field is added to the Organization schema to track the most recently active organization.
* Automatic tracking is implemented when users switch organizations via `setActiveOrganization`.
* A helper hook is provided to automatically find and set the last-used organization as active during the sign-in process.

---

## 🔧 Changes Made

### Schema Changes
* Added `lastUsed: boolean` field to the Organization schema (default: `false`).
* Updated schema definition in `organization.ts`.

### Core Functionality
* **`setActiveOrganization` Route (`routes/crud-org.ts`):**
    * Sets `lastUsed: true` for the newly active organization.
    * Sets `lastUsed: false` for all other organizations belonging to the same user.
* **Organization Adapter:**
    * Added `findLastUsedOrganization` method, which queries for the organization where `lastUsed: true` for the current user.

### Helper Function
* **`setLastUsedOrganizationAsActive` (`utils.ts`):**
    * A utility function designed for use in `databaseHooks.session.create.after`.
    * It automatically finds and sets the `lastUsed` organization as active in the session upon sign-in.
    * Exported from the organization plugin for easy integration.

### Tests
* **Organization Switching Tests (`crud-org.test.ts`):** Ensure the `lastUsed` flag is updated correctly when switching.
* **Sign-in Tests (`sign-in.test.ts`):** Verify the automatic setting of the last-used organization on sign-in.

---
**Database Migration Required ⚠️**
This feature requires a mandatory database migration.

A new field has been introduced to the Organization schema to support the last-used tracking functionality. You must run a migration script against your database to add this column before deploying this update

          await setLastUsedOrganizationAsActive(session, ctx, orgPlugin.options);
        },
      },
    },

items.title: feat(organization)!: add email confirmation for organization deletion
items.body: ## Summary Adds optional email confirmation before an organization is deleted (`organizationDeletion`), with a `confirmationMode: "explicit"` option so the emailed link can't delete an organization just by being opened. Closes #11530 ## Problem `organization.delete` deletes the organization as soon as the permission check passes. There is no confirmation step, even though `user.deleteUser` already has an optional email confirmation. Deleting an organization is irreversible, so it's the one place in the plugin where I'd expect the same opt-in protection. ## Changes - `organizationDeletion.sendDeleteOrganizationVerification` (opt-in). With it configured, the first `organization.delete` call creates a single-use token scoped to `(organization, requesting user)`, emails a link, and returns `{ success: true, message: "Verification email sent" }` instead of deleting. `deleteTokenExpiresIn` sets the lifetime (default one day). - `confirmationMode`: - `"instant"` (default): `GET /organization/delete/callback` re-checks everything and deletes, through the existing path including `beforeDeleteOrganization` / `afterDeleteOrganization`. - `"explicit"`: the link is the app's own URL, and the app calls `GET /organization/delete/preview` then `POST /organization/delete/confirm`, so a link prefetcher or scanner can't delete anything by opening the email. - `organization.delete` also accepts the `token` in its body, like `user.deleteUser`, which is why `organizationId` becomes optional in the body (the token carries it). - The token is validated first and only consumed right before the deletion, after the session, membership, `organization:delete` permission and `disableOrganizationDeletion` are re-checked, so an unauthenticated or unauthorized visit doesn't burn it. It is bound to `(organization, user)` and records the mode it was issued for. - Preview, confirm, callback and the `token` body path read the session through `getAuthoritativeSessionFromCtx`, so a revoked session that an earlier hook loaded from the cookie cache can't authorize a deletion. I reproduced this with a test before fixing it. - The `GET` callback refuses an `"explicit"` token, so a `callbackURL` that names another trusted host serving the same auth routes can't turn it into a one-click deletion. The refusal happens before the token is consumed, so it stays usable for `confirm`. - In explicit mode `callbackURL` must be an absolute URL that doesn't lead back to the instant callback (however its path is encoded) and doesn't already carry a `token` parameter. It's checked before the token is created, so a rejected request leaves no orphaned row. This uses the same small helper, `utils/confirmation-url.ts`, as the delete-user, change-email and transfer-ownership PRs; the file is identical in all of them. It canonicalizes the base URL's path the same way as the target's, so a base URL with encoded or repeated segments still compares equal. - `appendQueryParams` is ported from `main` into `@better-auth/core/utils/url` (first commit), since `next` doesn't have it yet and the link building uses it. It's the same function, so it won't conflict when `main` is merged into `next`. - The deletion itself moved into a shared `performDeleteOrganization`, used by the immediate path, the callback and `confirm`. - The `ORGANIZATION_DELETION_DISABLED` error is now defined with the plugin's other error codes, with the same code and message as before. - The docs also fix a pre-existing inaccuracy: the Delete Organization section described the top-level `disableOrganizationDeletion` as if it lived under `organizationDeletion`. This PR targets `next` because of the breaking type change below (the changeset is `minor`). The change is built on `next`, so the diff only contains its own commits. The sibling PRs (delete-user, change-email, transfer-ownership) are `patch` changes against `main`. ## Breaking change (types only) `organization.delete` now returns `Organization | { success: true; message: string }`, since the pending-verification response can't return the deleted organization. At runtime nothing changes for anyone who doesn't configure `organizationDeletion`, but code that reads the result without narrowing it (for example `.slug`) needs a type guard. If you'd rather avoid that, I can look at a non-breaking shape (for example a return type that only becomes the union when `sendDeleteOrganizationVerification` is configured). As it's set up now it goes through `next` with the `!` and a `minor` changeset. Tell me which you prefer. ## Notes for review - No schema changes. It reuses the existing `verification` table. - `disableOrganizationDeletion` is top-level while `organizationDeletion` is nested. Moving it would be breaking, so I left it as is. - The immediate path (no confirmation configured) keeps reading the session as before. Only the new token endpoints and the `token` body path use the authoritative read. - For HTTP requests the origin of `callbackURL` is checked against `trustedOrigins` by the existing origin middleware; direct `auth.api` calls skip that, which the docs call out. - The token is consumed before the deletion runs, so a hook that vetoes the deletion means the owner requests a new link. That keeps a link redeemable at most once under concurrency. ## Tests In `crud-org.test.ts`: - instant mode sends an email and only deletes after the callback; explicit mode previews without deleting and `confirm` applies it - the callback is rejected once the caller's delete permission was revoked, or once deletion was disabled after the token was issued - the token isn't consumed by a visit with no session, a token for one organization can't delete another, and it's single-use under concurrency - another member with the delete permission can't use someone else's token, and the attempt doesn't burn it; unknown and expired tokens are rejected - a revoked session with a valid cached cookie is rejected by preview, confirm, callback and the `token` body path (with a hook that preloads the session) - missing, relative, callback-pointing (plain, trailing slash, percent-encoded, dot segments) and `token`-carrying `callbackURL`s are rejected and leave no token - an explicit-mode token can't be redeemed through the GET callback, and it still works afterwards for `confirm` Plus unit tests for the URL helper and the client signals. ## Changeset `better-auth`: `minor`, with the breaking type change called out. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds optional email confirmation before an organization is deleted, mirroring `user.deleteUser`'s existing `sendDeleteAccountVerification` and closing #11530. When `organizationDeletion.sendDeleteOrganizationVerification` is configured, `organization.delete` emails a single-use confirmation link instead of deleting immediately and returns `{ success: true, message: "Verification email sent" }`. `confirmationMode` defaults to `instant`, where the emailed `GET` link deletes on visit after re-checking the session, membership, and `organization:delete` permission. Set it to `explicit` so the link only previews the deletion and the app applies it with `POST /organization/delete/confirm`, keeping mail clients and link scanners from deleting an organization by opening the email. Without the option, deletion behaves exactly as before. **Security hardening** - The token is consumed only right before deletion, so a visit with no session or revoked permission doesn't burn it. - Once consumed, the token is spent: a hook vetoing the deletion leaves the org intact, but a failure in the deletion itself or `afterDeleteOrganization` may already have removed it, so check whether it still exists before asking for a new link. - The confirmation email is sent through background tasks; sender failures are logged and don't fail the request. - The token is bound to `(organization, user)`, single-use under concurrency, and explicit-mode tokens are refused by the `GET` callback. - Token endpoints re-read the session from the store, so a revoked session loaded from the cookie cache can't authorize a deletion. - Explicit mode requires an absolute `callbackURL` that can't lead back to the instant callback or already carry a `token`, validated before the token is created. **Breaking change (types only)** - `organization.delete` now returns `Organization | { success: true; message: string }`; code reading the result without narrowing (for example `.slug`) needs a type guard. Written for commit eb32ec5386ce067af3287dda5c52de71312547ed. Summary will update on new commits.
